title: Contracted out although the department says City staff have the skills
question: In how many requests does the department itself say that City job classes or its own employees could do the work?
finding: Of 865 request forms read, 181 ($1.79 billion) answer that City job classes or the department’s own employees have the skills: on the newer form, 164 of 242 answers to “Does City have classifications with the required specialized skills” are yes. A further 225 older forms name the civil-service classes that “normally perform” the work. The largest of the first kind: Public Health $162.6 million (Behavioral health services in locked facilities); Public Health $86.2 million (Mental Health Services Act Peer Programs); Public Utilities Commission $75.0 million (PRO.0333 As Needed Environmental Services). Across all forms, 40 requests ($726.5 million) give vacancies, attrition, a hiring freeze or too few staff as a reason for going outside; 8 mention the freeze.
how: Read from the request forms (“PSC Form 1”). Newer forms (ServiceNow, from 2024) ask Q5c and Q5e directly; older forms ask which civil-service classes normally perform the work (question 3B). A row is shown where Q5c or Q5e is “Yes”, or where question 3B names class numbers; rows where the department itself says yes come first. Staffing reasons are found by searching the text of each form (its first pages) for vacancies, attrition, a hiring freeze, frozen positions or too few staff.
limits: Naming the class that normally does the work is what the old form asks for, and a department can still contract out for peaks in workload, short projects, specialist equipment, or work the Charter or a grant requires to go outside; the Commission reviews and the unions are notified. A “yes” is a question for the next record (the department’s reasons and the vacancy count in those classes), not a finding.
